# Introduction

We work Section 5.1.1 from [the textbook](#r1).

# Packages

First we load the relevant packages to our notebook session.

```{r}
library(glmnet) # for ridge and lasso
library(ISLR2) #package contains the data files, but not this one
library(mbadtools) # used to manipulate data and plot
```

# Data

We load the `Advertising` data from the csv file using Import Dataset, and preserve the code to load it here.

```{r}
library(readr)
Advertising <- read_csv("Advertising.csv")
```

# Data Display

```{r}
Advertising %>% skim
Advertising %>% glimpse
data=Advertising #copy the data set to a new name
```

There are 200 observations and 5 columns. The first column just identifies each observation. There are no missing entries.

# Validation

Validation involves taking a random sample of the data to train a model on, and then testing the model against different data. We have to set up a training and test dataset from the 200 observations we are given in Advertising.  

Why do we do this? We want a model we select to be **robust**. That means it would be good at giving predictions on data it has not seen before.  In validation we simulate that, by testing on different data from what we trained on.

# Set Seed

We do this whenever we need to do random sampling. If we don't do it, we get
different results every time we run the code.   For creating a sample notebook, we want the results to be reproducible by someone else.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
```

# Create train and test records

We sample 100 random numbers without replacement from the 200 (for the 200 observations in the dataset).

```{r}
# choose 100 random numbers from 1 to 200
train = sample(200, 100)
train
```

The test data will be the row numbers not in the vector `train`.

# Make a category variable

We will classify variable `Sales` from a continuous variable into a category variable of
Low and High Sales. There are a lot of ways to do this and here is one. We make a 0-1 variable for Low/High sales. 1 is High Sales and 0 is Low Sales, 1 is bigger than mean, 0 is lower than mean.

Every ad is above average!!!!????? Lake Wobegone advertising.

The new column `SalesType` will be the classification variable, and will be 0 or 1. It checks whether data$Sales is larger than or equal to the mean, a logical (TRUE-FALSE) result, and multiplies it by 1 to make it a number, 0 or 1.

```{r}
data$SalesType = (data$Sales>=mean(data$Sales))*1
```

# Create train and test data

Separate data into test and train datasets.

```{r}
testdata = data[-train,]
traindata =data[train,]
```

Look them over.

```{r}
traindata
testdata
```

# Logistic regression to predict SalesType

We will use logistic regression to predict Low and High Sales. We run the classification regression using only the `TV` driver, on the training data to get the 'coefficients' to make the predictions.

```{r}
model1 = glm(SalesType ~ TV, data=traindata, family = binomial)
summary(model1)
```

# Prediction for test data

Remember we trained the logistic regression on the `traindata`. That is in `model1`. But we use `model1` to predict on the test data! That is what we mean by validation!!!  We use the `predict` function to get the predictions for test data. There is no `augment` function for `glm`.

```{r}
model1.prediction = predict(model1, data=testdata, type="response")
```

The `model1.prediction` is now a probability, we classify it as High (1) if the
probability >= 0.5. This corresponds to assuming that `SalesType` is equally
likely(in the absence of any information) to be Lo or HI. This is called the
prior probability of Low or High sales. We could also do it like this, which would be easier to read and explain.

```{r}
model1.prediction.type = case_when(model1.prediction >= 0.5 ~1, .default=0)
```

# Make a crosstab

We put the results into a table of Predicted (rows) and Observed (columns). Order in the `table()` function matters. We label the predicted and observed, with the 'dnn' parameter. It's nice to add the sums of the rows and columns.

```{r}
tab = table(testdata$SalesType, model1.prediction.type, dnn=c("Observed","Predicted")
      , deparse.level = 2)
tab %>% addmargins
```

This structure is often called a confusion matrix, frequently used in classification. 
```{r}
cm = conf_mat(
  data.frame(Salestype=as.factor(testdata$SalesType),
             Prediction=as.factor(model1.prediction.type)
             ),
  truth=Salestype, estimate=Prediction)
cm
```

# Prediction Error

Now we see what error we made. We can use the mean value of the cases where
Predicted==Observed, because they are 0-1 variables. It would be more
complicated if they were other types of data. In the `yardstick` package, part of `mbadtools`, we have generic functions to compute metrics like `accuracy`.

```{r}
model1.prediction.error = mean(model1.prediction.type != testdata$SalesType)
model1.prediction.error
a1 = accuracy_vec(factor(testdata$SalesType),
             factor(model1.prediction.type)
             )
1-a1 # the error will be 1 - accuracy
```

If we want to know how often the prediction was right, we can compute the *accuracy*, which is given by the formula

```{r}
model1.prediction.accuracy = mean(model1.prediction.type == testdata$SalesType)
a1
```

It tells us the prediction of the test result was right 56% of the time. We can speculate as analysts whether this result is good enough to become a reliable method for the business. 

Or we can do this and get lots more metrics.
```{r}
cm %>% summary()
```


# Another LR

We will use a different logistic regression to predict Low and High Sales. This one uses `TV` and `Radio`.  Run it on `traindata` to get `model2.`

```{r}
model2 = glm(SalesType ~ TV + Radio, data=traindata, family = binomial)
summary(model2)
```

# Prediction and accuracy calculation

Use the `model2` and `predict` function to get prediction for test data.

```{r}
# predictions
model2.prediction = predict(model2, testdata, type="response")
model2.prediction.type = case_when(model2.prediction >= 0.5 ~ 1, .default = 0)
# table
tab2=table(model2.prediction.type, testdata$SalesType, dnn=c("Predicted","Observed")
      , deparse.level = 2) 
tab2 %>% addmargins
# confusion matrix
cm2 = conf_mat(
  data.frame(Salestype=as.factor(testdata$SalesType),
             Prediction=as.factor(model2.prediction.type)
             ),
  Salestype, Prediction)
cm2
# accruacy
model2.prediction.accuracy = mean(model2.prediction.type == testdata$SalesType)
cat("\nAccuracy: ", model2.prediction.accuracy)
cat("\n")
accuracy_vec(factor(testdata$SalesType), factor(model2.prediction.type))
# confusion matrix metrics
cm2 %>% summary()
```

The prediction accuracy is much higher here. Now the prediction error is only 5%. Adding the second predictor made a big difference.

Balanced accuracy is another frequently used metric. We could see it in the metrics above.
```{r}
bal_accuracy_vec(factor(testdata$SalesType), factor(model2.prediction.type))
```

# Conclusion

The second model appears to do quite well on the test data. It might be a candidate for production use.

We learned how to run and evaluate a classification regression using a validation strategy. We chose 50% of the data for training the model, and then tested on the other half.

This is a simple picture of how to improve robustness by selecting a more robust model that performs better on data it has not been trained on.
